newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-AMMB year net exceeds forecasts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-AMMB year net exceeds forecasts.

text.p: Malaysian banking and finance group AMMB Holdings Bhd's 71.16 percent rise in net profit for the year to March 31, 1997 was better than expected, analysts said on Wednesday.
The group announced a net profit of 559.7 million ringgit ($223.9 million) for the period, compared to 327.0 million ringgit in 1995/96.
A poll of 34 analysts by Edinburgh Financial Publishing's Estimates Directory in April had projected the earnings at 475.9 million ringgit.
"The results are ahead of my expectations, primarily because of the securities side (of the operations)," said Simon Maughan, head of research at W.I. Carr in Kuala Lumpur.
The group is one of Malaysia's largest banking and finance supermarkets.
The group's stockbroking activities, mainly contributed to by Arab-Malaysian Securities Bhd posted a pre-tax profit of 191.14 million ringgit in 1997, against 73.35 million ringgit in 1996.

"There is a tendency for banks to hold back on their profits for following years. But I think they (AMMB) are trying to impress upon the market that there is nothing wrong with the group," said Maughan.
Share prices of banking and finance companies had come under severe pressure in March following curbs by Malaysia's central Bank Negara on lending for property and share acquisitions.
AMMB Holdings share price has fallen from a high of 24 ringgit on March 13, to 16.40 at the close of trading on Wednesday.

Bank Negara has stipulated that banks would not be able to lend more than 20 percent of their total loan portfolio to 'less productive' property ventures such as private developments. There is no restriction on lending to infrastructure projects.
The company said in May its exposure to property and share financing was within the limits stipulated by Bank Negara.
AMMB said on Wednesday real estate lending accounted for 23.2 percent of its total loans on a group basis, which included both productive and less-productive lending.

"Although their exposure to property lending is high, property loans is their niche, and they are experts at managing the risk associated with the sector," said Ngu Chie Kieng, research analyst at T.A. Securities in Kuala Lumpur.
"People were selling down the shares in March because they were not sure about the country due to its exposure to property, not because there was anything wrong with the company," said Ngu.

AMMB's banking activities also posted better-than-expected gains, said analysts. The merchant banking segment reported a pre-tax profit of 300.83 million ringgit in 1997, compared to 221.60 million ringgit in 1996, while commercial banking jumped from 30.06 million to 80.10 million.
"The commercial bank's performance was very impressive," said Ngu.
Meanwhile, group firm Arab-Malaysian Finance Bhd reported a 39.3 percent rise in net profit to 251.67 million ringgit, aided by a 30.4 percent increase in lending for automobile purchases.
"With new car sales staying almost flat over the year, they must be taking market share away from everyone else," said Maughan.
